title_page.title: Estimating atrial fibrillation burden as a per-patient quantification problem with distribution-free uncertainty intervals: development and multinational external validation
title_page.article_type: Clinical Research Article (digital health / artificial intelligence)

runs.text: Abstract
Background and Aims

Atrial fibrillation (AF) burden is increasingly used to guide care, yet automated tools estimate it by counting windows classified as AF—a biased estimator of a proportion—and report no uncertainty. We aimed to develop and externally validate a detector-agnostic burden estimator that corrects this bias and provides per-patient uncertainty intervals.
Methods

Burden was framed as a per-patient quantification problem. A patient-adaptive hidden Markov quantifier (PA-HMMQ) re-estimates each patient's rhythm dynamics from the output of any beat-to-beat (RR) interval AF detector; split-conformal calibration yields 90% burden intervals. Three detectors were developed on 243 patients (4,045 h; six US databases) and validated, without retraining or recalibration, in 988 patients (8,576 h) from Japan, China and Canada. The pre-specified primary endpoint was the per-patient absolute burden error in pooled external cohorts.
Results

With the primary detector, the mean absolute burden error in external patients was 2.57 ± nan percentage points (pp) for PA-HMMQ versus 3.18 ± nan pp for classify-and-count (mean paired difference -0.60 pp, 95% CI -0.73 to -0.49; Holm-adjusted P = 0.008), and it was lower than all eight comparators, including established quantification and smoothing methods. Conformal intervals covered the reference burden in 0.928 of external patients (target 0.90) with a median width of 1.23 pp. The largest residual errors arose in patients with atrial flutter, which RR-based detectors classified as AF, and from false burden in AF-free patients.
Conclusion

Treating AF burden as a quantity to be estimated, rather than a count of classified windows, modestly but consistently reduced burden error across three continents and enabled calibrated uncertainty intervals. Flutter and false-positive burden in AF-free patients remain the main limitations of RR-based burden estimation.
Keywords
Atrial fibrillation burden • Ambulatory electrocardiography • Artificial intelligence • Uncertainty quantification • Conformal prediction • External validation
What's New?

AF burden was estimated as a per-patient proportion (quantification) instead of by counting AF-classified windows, using a patient-adaptive hidden Markov model that works on top of any RR-interval AF detector.

In 988 external patients from Japan, China and Canada, the method reduced the mean absolute burden error from 3.18 to 2.57 percentage points and was the most accurate of nine estimators, consistently across three detectors.
Distribution-free conformal intervals attained close to nominal 90% coverage in external cohorts, giving clinicians a per-patient statement of burden uncertainty.
Atrial flutter and false burden in AF-free patients were the dominant remaining error sources.
Introduction

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is increasingly characterised by how much of the time a patient spends in the arrhythmia rather than by its mere presence. AF burden—the proportion of monitored time in AF—is associated with ischaemic stroke and other outcomes, is an endpoint of rhythm-control trials, and has become central to the interpretation of device-detected subclinical AF
. The 2024 European Society of Cardiology guidelines acknowledge burden as a clinically relevant descriptor while noting that its measurement is method-dependent
. With the spread of long-term Holter, patch, wearable and implantable monitoring, burden is now almost always computed automatically.

Automated burden estimation is usually performed by running a window-level AF detector over the recording and counting the windows classified as AF. Beat-to-beat (RR) interval detectors range from classical irregularity statistics
and feature-based machine learning
to deep recurrent networks evaluated across geographies
. These studies report excellent window-level discrimination, but burden is a patient-level
proportion

, and counting classified windows is a biased estimator of a proportion whenever sensitivity and specificity are imperfect: false-positive windows inflate burden in patients with little AF, false negatives deflate it in patients with persistent AF, and the size of both errors changes with the patient's own AF prevalence
. Recent work has shown that burden derived from averaged detector probabilities degrades under external dataset shift unless probabilities are recalibrated with labelled data from the target cohort

. In addition, current tools report burden as a single number without an uncertainty statement, although a clinician deciding whether a low burden is real needs to know how wrong the estimate could plausibly be.
The machine-learning field of
quantification
addresses exactly the problem of estimating class proportions in a new sample whose prevalence differs from that of the training data
, and conformal prediction provides distribution-free uncertainty intervals with finite-sample coverage guarantees
. Neither has, to our knowledge, been applied to AF burden: conformal methods in electrocardiography have so far targeted diagnostic classification
, and quantification estimators assume independent samples, whereas rhythm windows are strongly dependent in time.

We therefore reformulated AF-burden estimation as a per-patient quantification problem and developed a detector-agnostic burden layer—a patient-adaptive hidden Markov model quantifier (PA-HMMQ) with distribution-free conformal burden intervals. We tested, in multinational external cohorts from Japan, China and Canada, (i) whether it reduces per-patient burden error compared with classify-and-count and established quantification and smoothing methods, (ii) whether its intervals attain their nominal coverage, and (iii) how robust it is to R-peak detection errors, ectopy and reduced training data.
Methods

## Study design and reporting This was a retrospective development and multinational external-validation study using publicly available, de-identified ambulatory electrocardiogram (ECG) databases. Reporting follows TRIPOD+AI
and the 2025 EHRA/HRS/ESC e-Cardiology scientific statement on artificial intelligence in clinical electrophysiology

; the EHRA AI checklist is provided as Supplementary material. The analysis plan, including hyper-parameters, random seeds, endpoints and statistical tests, was written and version-controlled before any model was trained (Supplementary material S1).
## Data sources The development pool comprised six PhysioNet databases recorded in the USA
: the Long-Term AF Database (LTAFDB)
, the MIT-BIH AF Database (AFDB), the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database (MITDB)
, the BIDMC Congestive Heart Failure Database (CHFDB)

, and the MIT-BIH Normal Sinus Rhythm databases (NSRDB, NSR2DB). External validation used three cohorts that were never used for training, calibration or tuning: SHDB-AF, 24-h two-channel Holter recordings of Japanese patients with paroxysmal AF annotated beat-by-beat by a cardiologist
; CPSC2021, dynamic Holter recordings from the 4th China Physiological Signal Challenge
; and Icentia11k, single-lead patch recordings from Canadian outpatients with technologist-reviewed beat and rhythm labels

, from which 800 patients were sampled uniformly at random (fixed seed, without inspecting labels) and their first ten 70-min segments used. Only beat and rhythm annotation files were used (Supplementary Table S1 lists versions, licences and exclusions).

## Reference standard and units of analysis RR intervals were derived from the database beat annotations (automatic R-peak annotations for AFDB and SHDB-AF, reviewed annotations elsewhere); intervals outside 0.2–3.0 s or outside labelled rhythm segments were excluded. Each RR interval inherited the reference rhythm at its terminating beat. RR series were cut into non-overlapping windows of 60 consecutive valid intervals. A window was labelled AF if ≥50% of its duration was annotated AF. The reference AF burden of a patient was the AF-annotated time divided by the analysed time; atrial flutter was counted as non-AF (sensitivity analysis: AF+flutter). Recordings of the same patient were aggregated, so the unit of analysis was the patient.

## Window-level detectors Because the proposed method operates on any detector's output, three detectors spanning model complexity were trained: (i) Classical-LR, a logistic regression on three classical irregularity features (normalised RMSSD, Shannon entropy, turning-point ratio)

; (ii) LightGBM, gradient-boosted trees on 16 RR features including sample-entropy-based irregularity (pre-specified primary detector); and (iii) RRNet, a convolutional–bidirectional recurrent network on the normalised RR sequence, re-implemented in the spirit of ArNet/ArNet2
(architecture in Supplementary material). Each detector outputs a window probability

## Data partitioning and leakage control For each of five pre-specified seeds, development patients were split, stratified by database and AF presence, into training (45%; 15% of these for early stopping), calibration A (15%; all source calibration quantities), calibration B (20%; conformal quantile only) and test (20%) sets. No patient appeared in more than one set. An automated audit fingerprinting all RR windows and recordings across all databases identified one exact duplicate recording in SHDB-AF (two files of the same subject with identical RR series), which was removed (Supplementary Table S1). Features and RR normalisation were computed within each window only.

## Endpoints and statistical analysis The pre-specified primary endpoint was the per-patient absolute burden error (percentage points, pp) in the pooled external cohorts with the LightGBM detector. Per-patient errors were averaged over the five seeds and compared between the proposed estimator and each comparator using two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction across the eight comparators
; effect sizes are the mean and median paired differences with patient-level bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (2000 resamples) and matched-pairs rank-biserial correlations
. Secondary endpoints were Bland–Altman bias and limits of agreement
, Lin's concordance correlation coefficient

, false burden in AF-free patients, classification of patients by burden thresholds (≥30 s of AF, ≥1%, ≥10%; exact McNemar tests on seed-majority classifications), conformal coverage (Clopper–Pearson 95% CI) and interval width, and window-level discrimination and calibration of the detectors. Summary statistics are mean ± standard deviation over seeds. Robustness was assessed by re-analysing SHDB-AF after simulated missed R peaks (2%, 5%), false R peaks (2%, 5%), R-peak timing jitter (10, 25 ms) and premature beats with compensatory pauses (5%, 10%). Sensitivity analyses varied κ, the training-set size (25%, 50%) and the window length (30, 120 beats). Analyses used Python 3.13 with PyTorch, scikit-learn, LightGBM and SciPy; all code and the commands regenerating every number, table and figure are publicly available (Data availability).

## Ethics Only publicly available, de-identified databases distributed under open licences were used; the original studies obtained ethical approval and consent as described in the cited publications. No new data were collected, so additional ethical approval and consent were not required.
Results

## Cohorts The development pool comprised 243 patients (4,045 h of analysed RR data; 119 with AF), and the external cohorts 988 patients (8,576 h; 175 with AF and 39 with atrial flutter): SHDB-AF 93 patients (72 with AF during the recording), CPSC2021 105 patients and Icentia11k 790 patients (50 with AF) (Table 1; Supplementary Figure S1). Ten of the 800 sampled Icentia11k patients had no analysable labelled windows.

## Window-level detection All three detectors discriminated AF windows well in every cohort (Supplementary Table S2, Supplementary Figures S2–S3). For LightGBM, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.997 ± nan in the development test set and 0.973 ± nan, 0.992 ± nan and 0.990 ± nan in SHDB-AF, CPSC2021 and Icentia11k; sensitivity and specificity at the default threshold were 0.895 and 0.953 in SHDB-AF and 0.979 and 0.970 in Icentia11k.

## Burden estimation By the pre-specified development-data rule (Amendment A1), the PA-HMMQ variant using the detector probability as emission likelihood had a lower development error (1.381 vs 1.938 pp) and was designated the final method; the pre-registered calibrated-emission variant is reported alongside.

With the primary LightGBM detector, the final PA-HMMQ had the lowest mean absolute burden error of all estimators in the development test set and in each external cohort (Table 2, Figure 2): 4.35 ± nan pp in SHDB-AF, 3.39 ± nan pp in CPSC2021 and 2.26 ± nan pp in Icentia11k, compared with 4.72 ± nan, 4.86 ± nan and 2.77 ± nan pp for classify-and-count. In the pooled external cohorts the error was 2.57 ± nan pp versus 3.18 ± nan pp for classify-and-count, 2.88 ± nan pp for median-filtered counting, 2.87 ± nan pp for a hidden Markov model with fixed dynamics and 4.65 ± nan pp for isotonic-recalibrated probability averaging. In the primary paired analysis, the final PA-HMMQ reduced the per-patient error relative to every comparator (Table 4; Supplementary Figure S6); the mean paired reduction was -0.60 pp (95% CI -0.73 to -0.49) versus classify-and-count and -0.29 pp (95% CI -0.43 to -0.17) versus the fixed-dynamics HMM (Holm-adjusted P ≤ 0.008 for all comparators). Because most external patients were AF-free and many estimators returned exactly zero burden for them, the median paired difference was close to zero; the improvement was concentrated in patients with AF (3.81 vs 4.52 pp) and in AF-free patients with false-positive windows (mean false burden 2.31 vs 2.89 pp; Table 3).

The ranking was reproduced with the Classical-LR and RRNet detectors (Supplementary Tables S3–S4): pooled external error 8.13 ± nan vs 9.04 ± nan pp (Classical-LR) and 4.01 ± nan vs 4.63 ± nan pp (RRNet). Agreement statistics are given in Table 3 and Figure 3: bias was 1.85 pp (classify-and-count 2.32 pp) and Lin's concordance correlation 0.904 (0.900). Patient classification by burden thresholds is reported in Supplementary Table S7.

## Ablation Supplementary Table S5 and Supplementary Figure S5 decompose the gain. Per-patient prior adaptation without a temporal model (EMQ) did not improve on classify-and-count externally (2.98 pp), whereas a temporal model with fixed source dynamics did (2.87 pp with calibrated emissions; 2.57 pp with probability emissions). Adding per-patient adaptation of the dynamics changed the error to 2.57 pp with probability emissions. The error varied little across prior strengths κ from 1 to 100 (Supplementary Table S5). With calibration-set emission histograms, the PA-HMMQ was not better than the fixed-dynamics HMM (2.87 vs 2.87 pp).

## Uncertainty intervals Normalised conformal intervals around the final PA-HMMQ covered the reference burden in 0.857 of development test patients and 0.928 (95% CI 0.910–0.943) of external patients (0.806 SHDB-AF, 0.876 CPSC2021, 0.949 Icentia11k), with a median width of 1.23 pp (Table 5, Figure 4). Coverage was lower in patients with AF (0.851) than in AF-free patients (0.945). Constant-width conformal intervals around classify-and-count were wider (median 3.20 pp) with coverage 0.870, and the uncalibrated posterior credible intervals under-covered (0.854).

## Robustness and sensitivity analyses In SHDB-AF, all estimators deteriorated with false R peaks and simulated premature beats, while missed beats and timing jitter had smaller effects (Figure 5; Supplementary Table S9). Training on 25% or 50% of the training patients and using 30- or 120-beat windows are reported in Supplementary Table S11.

## Error analysis Errors were concentrated in patients with intermediate burden and in a small number of patients with atrial flutter (Figure 6; Supplementary Tables S6, S13). Of the 988 external patients, 39 had flutter; counting flutter as arrhythmia reduced the error of the final PA-HMMQ to 1.66 pp, and excluding these patients (post hoc) to 1.24 pp (classify-and-count 2.24 and 1.84 pp; Supplementary Table S8). Absolute error correlated with the proportion of flutter (Spearman ρ = 0.297) and with the reference burden (ρ = 0.471), and only weakly with ectopic beats (supraventricular ρ = 0.037; ventricular ρ = 0.216; Supplementary Figure S7). Error did not differ materially by sex or age in SHDB-AF (Supplementary Table S12).

## Computational cost On a 4-core CPU, the final PA-HMMQ added a median of 244 ms per 24-h recording to detector inference (LightGBM 12 ms; RR-feature extraction 797 ms), and 288 ms including posterior sampling for the interval (Supplementary Figure S8).
Discussion

This study reframed automated AF-burden estimation as a per-patient quantification problem and showed, in 988 patients from three continents who contributed 8,576 hours of ambulatory recordings, that a patient-adaptive hidden Markov quantifier reduced burden error relative to classify-and-count and eight established alternatives, consistently across three detectors of very different complexity, and that conformal calibration turned its posterior uncertainty into intervals with close to nominal coverage outside the development population.
## Interpretation Two mechanisms explain the gain. First, burden is a property of a patient's rhythm
trajectory

: an isolated AF-like window inside long sinus rhythm, or a short regular stretch inside persistent AF, is more likely a classification error than a rhythm change. A temporal model therefore removes much of the window-level noise that classify-and-count propagates into burden, which is why median filtering and the fixed-dynamics HMM already improved on counting. Second, rhythm dynamics differ between patients—from AF-free to paroxysmal to persistent—and the source dynamics learned from a development population act as a prior that is wrong for many individual patients; re-estimating them per patient is the temporal analogue of prior-shift correction in quantification

. The ablation indicates that, in these data, most of the improvement came from the temporal model with sharp emission likelihoods, while per-patient adaptation contributed a smaller, consistent increment.
Two negative findings are informative. Recalibrating window probabilities on source patients (PCC-iso) made burden estimates
worse

in every cohort. A probability calibrated on a development population embeds that population's AF prevalence and pulls every patient's estimate towards it; good classifier calibration is therefore not sufficient for unbiased prevalence estimation, consistent with quantification theory
and complementary to the observation that target-cohort recalibration with labelled data restores probability-based burden

. Likewise, the pre-registered emission model—class-conditional histograms on calibration patients—flattened the likelihood ratios because window labels near rhythm transitions are noisy, letting sticky source dynamics over-smooth genuine rhythm changes; this is why the simpler probability-emission variant performed better, a choice made on development data only.
## Clinical implications AF burden is increasingly used to stratify risk and to evaluate therapy
, and device- or patch-derived burden informs decisions about subclinical AF

. An absolute error of a few percentage points matters most near decision-relevant thresholds and in patients with low burden, where false-positive windows from ectopy can create apparent AF. The proposed layer requires no retraining of an existing detector, adds milliseconds of computation per 24-h recording, and supplies an interval that tells the reader whether a reported burden of, for example, 2% is distinguishable from zero or from 10%. Because coverage is guaranteed only for patients exchangeable with the calibration set, the intervals should be recalibrated locally when a device or population differs substantially, as recently argued for AI-ECG classifiers
## Comparison with previous work Deep RR-interval models such as ArNet and ArNet2
and feature-based pipelines
reported strong window-level performance and low burden error, and commercial AI burden agrees closely with manual assessment in selected cohorts

. Those studies report point estimates only; the present work is complementary, operating on top of any such detector, and adds bias correction and patient-level uncertainty. Consistent with ArNet2, atrial flutter was the dominant failure mode of RR-based burden estimation

: flutter with variable conduction produces irregular RR intervals indistinguishable from AF without atrial activity information. Whether flutter time should count towards burden is partly definitional—stroke prevention recommendations for flutter largely follow those for AF
—and with an AF+flutter reference the errors of all estimators fell substantially.

## Limitations First, the study used retrospective public databases with heterogeneous annotation processes; reference labels, particularly in the large Icentia11k cohort, may contain errors, and R peaks were taken from database annotations rather than from a uniform detector, although simulated R-peak errors were examined. Second, the development pool was modest (243 patients) and from one country, although this makes the external results more conservative. Third, the absolute improvement was modest (a mean of -0.60 pp versus classify-and-count), the per-patient median difference was near zero because most external patients were AF-free, and the benefit was concentrated in a minority of patients; the clinical value of this improvement for decisions was not tested. Fourth, the emission model of the final method was changed from the pre-registered specification on the basis of development data (Amendment A1); both versions are reported. Fifth, conformal coverage is marginal over patients and was lower in patients with AF than in AF-free patients; it is not guaranteed under distribution shift. Sixth, 60-beat windows limit resolution for episodes shorter than about 30–60 s. Seventh, Icentia11k was represented by a random subset of patients and segments, and the reduced-training and window-length analyses omitted Icentia11k for computational reasons. Finally, no outcome data were available, and photoplethysmography-based wearables, which are increasingly used for burden monitoring
, were not studied.
Conclusions

Estimating AF burden as a per-patient quantity with a patient-adaptive hidden Markov quantifier, rather than counting AF-classified windows, reduced burden error across Japanese, Chinese and Canadian cohorts and three different detectors, and conformal calibration provided per-patient intervals with close to nominal coverage. The approach is detector-agnostic and inexpensive, but flutter and false-positive burden in AF-free patients remain the main obstacles to accurate RR-based burden assessment and should be addressed before burden thresholds are applied clinically.

legend.text: Study pipeline. RR intervals derived from ambulatory ECG beat annotations are cut into 60-beat windows and scored by a window-level AF detector. The patient-adaptive hidden Markov quantifier (PA-HMMQ) treats the patient's window sequence as a two-state Markov chain whose rhythm dynamics are re-estimated for each patient (maximum-a-posteriori expectation–maximisation with a prior centred on source dynamics from calibration patients A), and returns the posterior expected burden. Posterior sampling gives a model-based standard deviation that is converted into a 90% conformal interval using calibration patients B. External cohorts are never used for training or calibration.
